claims.text: Single-phase solid-solution formation in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by an interplay between kinetic quenching and diffusional homogenization.
An intermediate cooling ramp after rapid heating allows sufficient atomic diffusion to reduce elemental segregation.
An intermediate cooling ramp favors formation of a uniform crystal structure.
Prolonged high-temperature conditions typically trigger phase separation.
Rapid heating followed by fast quenching often produces phase separation in these nanoparticles.
Rapid heating followed by fast quenching often produces elemental segregation in these nanoparticles.
Rapid heating followed by fast quenching often produces uncontrolled particle morphology.
Very rapid quenching kinetically traps metastable structures.
A moderate cooling rate enhances atomic mobility and homogenizes elemental distributions.
Elevated temperatures during rapid heating enable high configurational entropy.
Cooling too quickly freezes atoms into a disordered, compositionally inhomogeneous state.
Limited diffusion during controlled cooling overcomes local compositional fluctuations and prevents elemental segregation.
Long-range diffusion during slower or extended cooling leads to macroscopic phase separation.
Relative to immediate quenching, intermediate cooling will increase structural uniformity.
Relative to immediate quenching, intermediate cooling will reduce elemental segregation.
Relative to immediate quenching, intermediate cooling will increase the fraction of nanoparticles exhibiting the targeted single-phase crystal structure.
The applicable cooling interval permits atomic diffusion on a timescale shorter than secondary-phase nucleation but longer than in a conventional rapid quench.
The favorable cooling-rate threshold varies with alloy composition and thermal history.
